title: Experiential Health Promotion for Cervical Cancer Early Detection in Indonesian Islamic Study Communities: A Pilot Quasi-Experimental Evaluation
content: Cervical cancer is largely preventable through human papillomavirus vaccination, screening, and timely treatment of precancerous lesions, but early detection remains underused in many community settings. This pilot quasi-experimental study evaluated an experiential learning-based health promotion model for improving cervical cancer early detection knowledge and exploratory attitude-response indicators among adult women attending Islamic study communities in Padangsidimpuan, Indonesia. The field evaluation used an uncontrolled one-group pretest-posttest design. Item refinement was conducted before final scoring to strengthen psychometric defensibility. The refined knowledge checklist retained 9 statistically valid baseline items, while the refined exploratory attitude-response scale retained 9 items that were valid and internally reliable at pretest and posttest. Complete paired data were available for 103 respondents. Refined knowledge scores increased from 6.09 +/- 2.04 to 6.54 +/- 1.09 out of 9 (mean difference = 0.46; 95% CI: 0.03-0.88; p = 0.037; Cohen's dz = 0.21). Refined attitude-response scores increased from 27.50 +/- 4.69 to 30.64 +/- 4.25 out of 36 (mean difference = 3.15; 95% CI: 1.91-4.38; p < 0.001; Cohen's dz = 0.50). The findings indicate that experiential health promotion was associated with immediate improvements in refined educational outcomes. Because the study was uncontrolled and measured short-term outcomes, controlled longitudinal evaluation with verified screening uptake is required before definitive effectiveness claims are made.
